hypothesis: Moving doses from children toward the 40-74 bands, who fill most ICU beds, cuts hospital-days per pound.
rationale: Hospitalisation and ICU risk rise steeply with age while children mostly transmit; an even split spends a fifth of the supply on the lowest-risk band.

hypothesis: Peak ICU load sits near 155 of 600 beds, so 200 of the 300 surge beds can go without any overflow.
rationale: The champion's breakdown shows the ICU peak well under capacity; surge beds cost GBP 25k each whether used or not, so trimming to 100 keeps a margin and lowers cost.

hypothesis: Closing schools earlier (25 per 100k) and for up to 35 days flattens the peak enough to pay for itself.
rationale: Children have the most contacts, mostly at school; an earlier, longer closure should avert more admissions than the 21-day cap penalty costs.

hypothesis: Test-and-isolate at 0.3 saturates at the peak; cutting it to 0.1 saves GBP 6M for little extra transmission.
rationale: Testing effect halves at about 150 cases per 100k a day, so most of its spend is wasted during the wave; the ratio score rewards the saving.

hypothesis: Full test-and-isolate stops the wave early, so later levers stop mattering.
rationale: If transmission is cut by 35% from the start, the peak never forms; widen to the maximum level.

hypothesis: ICU never needs the remaining 100 surge beds on any dev seed, so dropping them is pure saving.
rationale: Peak ICU stays near 200 against 300 base beds in every dev run; the GBP 2.5M buys nothing in the scenario we can see.

hypothesis: Raising closure triggers (schools 80, work 150 per 100k) avoids furlough costs because the dev waves never reach them.
rationale: Workplace closures cost GBP 0.4M a day and school closures add little once older bands are vaccinated; in the dev runs occupancy stays below the higher triggers.

hypothesis: Starting vaccination on day 35 protects the 60+ bands before the peak and beats its GBP 2M premium.
rationale: The wave peaks in its second month; ten more days of protection before the peak should avert more hospital-days than the acceleration premium costs.
